payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image visibly use a chalk-like drawing medium, rather than merely having grain, blur, or smudging?
node.criteria: pass: affirmative visible chalk-like marks or material treatment establish a chalk medium; fail: visible evidence establishes a different medium or treatment without chalk; unknown: grain, smudging, or other cues are suggestive but do not resolve the medium.
node.binding: Assess only visible evidence of chalk-like medium or treatment; do not infer chalk from generic texture or from drawing style.

n3: The binding is malformed and underspecified (`a (...) been transformed`), which can destabilize the requested-change judgment. Make the node’s binding clearly identify the edited image and the full instruction: conversion of the scene into a chalk drawing. Preserve the distinction between chalk-like surface texture and drawing-form conversion: the edited image shows powdery/grainy, softened treatment, but the giraffes retain detailed, photo-like rendering, so this is evidence of progress without complete fulfillment—not proof that no change occurred. Keep the existing support-based partial rule and require affirmative evidence for a failed criterion; do not treat mere lack of decisive evidence as absence. The repeated `Unknown required evidence dependency` traces are a routing/schema or dependency-resolution failure, not visual evidence: ensure the node can consume valid saved support results and distinguish an unavailable/transport-failed support from a valid fail. The transport error in one trace must remain unresolved rather than count as negative evidence. Repeated variation in the chalk-medium assessment is a robustness signal, not grounds to dismiss the visible treatment or lower the requested standard.

Repair the binding so it unambiguously evaluates whether the depicted scene has been rendered as a drawing, while keeping medium texture distinct from drawing form. The edited image visibly has chalky grain, softened/streaked backgrounds, and altered color, but the giraffes retain detailed, photo-like shading and structure; these are signs of partial progress, not complete conversion. Preserve the criterion that surface effects alone do not establish drawing conversion, and do not let this support check turn a valid fail into a claim that no requested change occurred—the aggregate rubric handles partial progress. Keep fail dependent on affirmative evidence that the content remains photographic, and reserve unknown for genuinely indeterminate visual evidence. Separately, ensure the node’s routing/schema can consume valid support results and distinguish dependency or transport failures from visual judgments; the transport-failed trace is unresolved, not negative evidence. Repeated high-confidence fail judgments are consistent, while the single transport failure is an execution issue rather than evidence to alter the visual criterion.
